questions.question: What three qualities does the article say the work you choose to pursue needs to have?
questions.referenceAnswer: It needs to be something you have a natural aptitude for, that you have a deep interest in, and that offers scope to do great work.

questions.premise: The article says you don't need to worry much about whether a field offers scope for great work, since ambitious people are already too conservative on that score.
questions.question: What does the article recommend doing if you're not yet sure what to work on?
questions.referenceAnswer: Guess — pick something and get going, since the way to figure out what to work on is by working, and it's fine if you guess wrong sometimes.

questions.premise: Figuring out what to work on happens through actually working, not through advance analysis.
questions.question: What kind of curiosity does the article say signals you've found the right thing to work on?
questions.referenceAnswer: An excessive curiosity — curiosity about something to a degree that would bore most other people.

questions.premise: Excessive curiosity is the sign of having found the right thing to pursue.
questions.question: What four steps does the article describe as the general process followed by nearly everyone who's done great work?
questions.referenceAnswer: Choose a field, learn enough to reach the frontier of knowledge in it, notice the gaps at that frontier, and explore the promising ones.

questions.premise: The third of these steps is noticing gaps at the frontier of knowledge.
questions.question: Why does the article say noticing these gaps takes skill?
questions.referenceAnswer: Because your brain naturally wants to ignore such gaps so it can keep a simpler model of the world.

questions.question: Instead of following a detailed plan, what strategy does the article say most people who've done great work actually use, calling it 'staying upwind'?
questions.referenceAnswer: At each stage do whatever seems most interesting and gives you the best options for the future, rather than deciding in advance and executing a fixed plan.

questions.premise: Staying upwind means choosing whatever seems most interesting at each stage rather than following a fixed plan.
questions.question: What kind of 'lie' does the article say is often permissible when starting a new project?
questions.referenceAnswer: It's okay to underestimate, in your own mind, how much work the project will actually take — as in thinking 'how hard could it be?'

questions.question: Of the two forms of procrastination the article distinguishes, which does it call far more dangerous?
questions.referenceAnswer: Per-project procrastination — putting off starting an ambitious project year after year, since the delays are measured in years rather than days.

questions.premise: Per-project procrastination, putting off an ambitious project for years, is the more dangerous kind.
questions.question: Why does the article say this kind of procrastination is hard to notice in yourself?
questions.referenceAnswer: Because it disguises itself as work — you're busy and industrious on something else, so it never sets off the alarm that idleness would.

questions.question: Using the example of writing a page a day, what does the article say is the key to benefiting from the compounding effect of work over time?
questions.referenceAnswer: Consistency — getting something done every day, rather than a lot on some days and nothing on others.

questions.question: Rather than merely trying to be good at your field, what does the article say you should aim to be?
questions.referenceAnswer: The best — the article argues that if you don't try to be the best, you won't even be good.

questions.premise: The article says you should aim to be the best rather than merely good.
questions.question: How does the article distinguish genuine style from affectation?
questions.referenceAnswer: Style is doing things in a distinctive way without trying to; affectation is trying to seem distinctive, which is really pretending to be someone other than yourself doing the work.

questions.premise: Affectation means, in effect, pretending someone other than you is doing the work.
questions.question: What does the article identify as the core of being earnest, the positive quality it recommends instead of affectation?
questions.referenceAnswer: Intellectual honesty — having an exceptionally sharp, unbiased eye for the truth.

questions.question: When work could be seen either as creation or as discovery, which does the article say you should err toward?
questions.referenceAnswer: Discovery — try thinking of yourself as a mere conduit through which the ideas take their natural shape.

questions.question: What image does the article use to describe how original thinkers generate new ideas?
questions.referenceAnswer: It compares them to an angle grinder throwing off sparks — original thinkers can't help throwing off new ideas about whatever they focus on.

questions.question: What two ways does the article distinguish for being comfortable enough to break the rules that block new ideas?
questions.referenceAnswer: Being 'aggressively independent-minded' (enjoying breaking rules, which gives you extra energy) and being 'passively independent-minded' (simply not caring about or noticing rules, as novices and outsiders often do).

questions.question: What does the article say matters even more than originality in solving problems?
questions.referenceAnswer: Originality in choosing which problem to work on in the first place — this is what distinguishes people who discover whole new fields.

questions.premise: Choosing the right problem matters even more than skill in solving it.
questions.question: Rather than planning a project in advance, what approach does the article recommend for developing it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Start with something small and simple, then evolve it through a series of successive versions, letting the final result become more ambitious than anything you could have planned.

questions.question: What advantages does the article say the young have, compared with the advantages of the old?
questions.referenceAnswer: The young have energy, time, optimism, and freedom, while the old have knowledge, efficiency, money, and power.

questions.question: Between having many colleagues and having very good ones, which does the article say matters more?
questions.referenceAnswer: Quality matters more — it's better, even necessary, to have one or two truly great colleagues than a building full of merely pretty good ones.
